hypothesis: If the claim holds, then across species the haploid (germ-nucleus) chromosome number n is mostly 6 to 16, fewer species have n below 6, and still fewer have n above 16.
pass_criterion: Using one n per species, all three of these hold: (a) at least 70% of species have 6 <= n <= 16; (b) fewer than 15% have n < 6; (c) the share with n > 16 is smaller than the share with n < 6.
fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if any of these holds: fewer than 50% of species have 6 <= n <= 16; the share with n > 16 is greater than or equal to the share with n < 6; or the share with n > 16 is 15% or more. Results that meet neither the pass nor the fail criteria count as not supported.
interpretation: 'Germ-nuclei' chromosome number means the reduced, gametic or haploid number n. Thompson wrote before polyploidy was well understood. Where a record gives only 2n, n is taken as 2n/2 for the diploid cytotype. The test uses one n per species, taking the modal or lowest recorded cytotype so that polyploid races are not counted as extra species. 'Few' and 'fewer still' are read as the two tails of the distribution, with the lower tail larger than the upper tail. Modern reinterpretation: polyploidy and dysploidy mean many angiosperms have n > 16, which is a real challenge to the claim. The dataset covers plants only, so this test decides the plant half of the claim. The animal half would need a separate animal karyotype dataset.

dataset.name: Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB)
dataset.why_it_fits: CCDB is a public compilation of chromosome counts across many land-plant species. Fields used: species name, gametophytic count (n), sporophytic count (2n), and the genus and family taxonomy. These give a per-species n distribution to compare with the 6–16 range. It does not cover animals.
